nameStory: The Bulbous Honey Fungus gets its 'honey' name from its golden-brown cap color that resembles amber honey, especially when young and fresh. The 'bulbous' part refers to the swollen, bulb-like base of its stem that helps distinguish it from its many honey mushroom relatives.
description: The Bulbous Honey Fungus is a medium-sized mushroom with a honey-colored cap covered in small, dark scales that give it a slightly rough appearance. It grows up to 4 inches across with a sturdy stem that can reach 4 inches tall and has a distinctive swollen base. This fungus is both a recycler of dead wood and an occasional troublemaker for living trees, breaking down forest debris while sometimes attacking weakened trees.

idTips.label: Stem Base
idTips.description: Look for the telltale bulbous, swollen base of the stem - this is the key feature that separates it from other honey mushrooms. The bulb feels firm and solid when gently squeezed.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Honey-brown to yellow-brown cap with small, darker scales scattered across the surface. The cap feels slightly rough to the touch due to these tiny scales and may have a subtle peachy or orange tint.

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: White to creamy gills that may develop pale orange tones with age. They're attached to the stem and feel soft when touched gently with a finger.

idTips.label: Ring
idTips.description: White, cobwebby ring around the upper stem that may be delicate and sometimes tears or disappears with age. The stem above the ring is pale orange to brown, while below it's lighter colored.

idTips.label: Smell
idTips.description: Often has a pleasant, slightly sweet or mushroomy smell, sometimes with faint honey-like notes. Some people detect a mild yeasty or bread-like aroma.

idTips.label: Spore Print
idTips.description: Produces white spores when a cap is placed gill-side down on dark paper overnight. This white spore print helps confirm it's in the honey mushroom group.

habitat: Found in New England's mixed and deciduous forests, particularly around oak, maple, and beech trees. Look for it growing from buried dead roots, old stumps, or at the base of dying trees in rich, moist woodland soil. It often appears in small clusters or scattered groups rather than large fairy rings.

seasonality.spring: Rarely fruits in spring, though the underground fungal network is actively growing and spreading through root systems and buried wood.
seasonality.summer: May begin producing small flushes of mushrooms during warm, wet periods, especially after heavy summer rains in July and August.
seasonality.fall: Peak fruiting season from September through October when cool, moist conditions trigger the main mushroom flush. This is the best time to find fresh specimens.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground mushrooms disappear, but the extensive underground network remains active under the soil and snow, continuing to decompose buried wood.

funFact: A single individual of this species in Michigan is considered one of the largest living organisms on Earth, weighing an estimated 400 tons and covering an area larger than 350 football fields - it's been quietly growing underground for about 2,500 years!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with other honey mushrooms, but the bulbous stem base is your key distinguishing feature - other honey mushrooms have straight, non-bulbous stems. Remember: 'Bulbous base, different case!' Also distinguished from deadly Destroying Angels, which are pure white and have bulbous bases but completely different coloring.
contextualKnowledge: This species has had a confusing scientific history and was previously known by different names including Armillaria bulbosa and Armillaria lutea. The honey mushroom group in general is notoriously difficult for even experts to identify to species level without microscopic examination.
compareHints: Unlike the common Honey Mushroom (Armillaria mellea), the Bulbous Honey Fungus has that distinctive swollen stem base and tends to be less aggressive as a tree parasite. While other honey mushrooms in New England have relatively straight, uniform stems, this species always shows some degree of basal swelling that you can feel with your fingers.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Honey mushroom (Armillaria mellea) is extremely difficult to distinguish from other Armillaria species in the field, as they're part of what scientists call a 'cryptic species complex' - they look virtually identical but are genetically distinct.
